sanjay: Hey team — trying to run nsys/nvprof inside a rootless k8s pod that uses nvidia-container-toolkit. Capture fails with permission errors when opening /dev/nvidia* and trace is empty. Anyone run into this?
laura: yup, ran this last week. rootless pods don't get the device node perms or CAP_SYS_ADMIN which nsys needs for kernel timelines. what error are you seeing?
sanjay: the nsys error is: `Error: Failed to open device /dev/nvidiactl: Permission denied` and nvprof prints `CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN` on launch. quick ls from the pod: `crw-rw---- 1 root video 195, 0 Mar 12 12:00 /dev/nvidia0`
mike: fwiw, nvprof/nsys need access to device nodes + sometimes tracefs or debugfs depending on what you're capturing. if the pod is rootless the container user can't read the nodes. two options: run privileged profiling pod, or do host-side capture attached to the container PID.
laura: examples: privileged profiling daemonset approach (fast to get traces):
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: profiler-priv
spec:
  hostPID: true
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 0
  containers:
  - name: profiler
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/nsight-systems:23.6
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /dev
      name: dev
  volumes:
  - name: dev
    hostPath:
      path: /dev
```
Then run `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=/data/trace` against the process on the host/cgroup.
nicole: if you can't do privileged, another approach is host-side attach: run nsys on the node and attach to the container pid. steps I used: find container PID on host `crictl ps` -> `crictl inspect` -> `pid`, then `nsys profile -p <pid> --output=/tmp/trace`. That avoids giving the container extra capabilities.
laura: also check nvidia-container-toolkit/CRI plugin config: if device files aren't being exposed to the container you won't see them. for device plugin we expect `--gpus=all` or `resources: nvidia.com/gpu` via k8s device plugin. rootless runtimes sometimes drop dev nodes.
sanjay: any tips for file permissions to avoid privileged? I could add an initContainer to chown the device nodes to non-root but that seems sketchy.
mike: initContainer trick is fragile and requires hostPath mount of /dev which itself needs privileges. For a safer non-priv route: run a small privileged helper DaemonSet that creates a character device in a shared emptyDir with mode 0666 (or uses `socat` proxy), then mount that into the profiling pod. Not ideal but used in labs.
nicole: also note that capturing kernel timelines showed lots of tiny kernel launches in our KV cache stress test — thousands of `gemm`/`kernelX` launches per second because batching window was too small. When I profiled earlier, the hot path was `cudaLaunchKernel` + `cudaMemcpyAsync` overhead, not just the expected fused-kernel time. We fixed that by increasing batching hold_time from 5ms -> 20ms and enabling request coalescing for small sequence lengths. That reduced kernel launch count and improved throughput.
laura: good point — metrics to look at in nsys timeline: kernel launch events, memcpy H2D/D2H, and stream synchronization spikes. Also check `nvtx` ranges if runtime annotates KV cache hits/misses — you can correlate missed-kv -> extra memcpy + kernel.
sanjay: I managed a host attach but the trace still showed a perf regression compared to last week: a new kernel variant is being selected (we saw `matmul_v2` instead of `matmul_v1`) with higher latency. Could that be from a changed filter in kernel-selection code?
mike: yes — kernel selector picks based on seq_len and dtype heuristics. if quantization profile changed or the input token distribution shifted small -> larger tiling chosen. Check the selector logs (enable DEBUG) and the model metadata used by the runtime. We had a regression where fallback to a generic kernel happened when `max_seq_len` was misreported.
laura: to reproduce: run nsys with cmdline and env dump to see which kernels and which kernel params were chosen. sample command we use: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt,nvtx -o /tmp/trace --force-overwrite --sampling-period=0.1 -- python3 run_inference.py --model xyz` capture the stdout for selector debug.
sanjay: thanks — what about perfetto in containers? I assume same device perms issue?
icole: perfetto needs tracefs and usually a host-side rolling collector. On nodes with perfetto from apt, create a hostPath mount of `/sys/kernel/tracing` and ensure trace_pipe is readable by the collector. Again requires privileges.
laura: TLDR / action items: 1) If you can, do host-side attach to avoid changing pod security. 2) If you need pod-local traces, run a short-lived privileged profiling pod/DS and mount /dev. 3) Check kernel-selector debug logs — we might have a regression causing a slower kernel variant. 4) Tune batching/window heuristics to reduce launch count (we saw big wins). 5) If anyone wants to reproduce reliably, I can drop a playbook that automates host-pid attach + selector debug env.
sanjay: @laura please drop the playbook. I'll try privileged pod on staging first. Thanks everyone :thumbsup:
infra-bot: NOTE: creating a profiling-privileged short-lived job requires SOC approval for node-level privileged jobs — file a quick infra request (link: https://internal/infra/requests)
